tip: Lowercase 'minggu' is week, but 'Minggu' with a capital M is Sunday: 'hari Minggu' = on Sunday, 'minggu depan' = next week. Case decides.
'Saja' softens suggestions: 'jam sepuluh saja' = let's just make it ten.
'Susah' + a 'di-' verb = hard to be X-ed: 'susah sekali ditelepon' = very hard to reach (lit. hard to be phoned). Same pattern: 'susah dicari' = hard to find.
'HP' (say: ha-pe) is the spoken word for phone: 'HP saya mati' = my phone died.
Storeys use plain numbers after 'lantai': 'lantai dua' = the second floor.
Adjectives follow the noun: 'mobil merah' = red car (lit. car red).
English needs 'has been broken since' – Indonesian just states the fact: 'rusak sejak kemarin sore' = broken since yesterday afternoon. No perfect tense exists.
'Tidak mau' + verb for things = won't: 'tidak mau menyala' = won't turn on.
The ending '-kan' turns a state into an action: 'menyala' = be on, 'nyalakan' = turn it on.
'Mematikan' = to turn off (lit. make dead): 'mematikan kompor' = turn off the stove.
With pairs, 'sebelah' means one of the two: 'hilang sebelah' = one of the pair is missing.
'Yang' picks out the specific one: 'meja kayu yang besar' = the big wooden table.
'Tua' darkens a color, 'muda' lightens it: 'merah tua' = dark red; 'biru muda' = light blue.
'Punya siapa?' = whose?: 'tas ini punya siapa?' = whose bag is this?
The 'ter-' at the front often describes a state: 'tergantung' = hanging; 'tertutup' = closed.
'Yang' links a noun to its description: 'hotel yang dekat' = a hotel that is near.
'Lebih ... daripada' = more ... than: 'lebih cepat daripada bus' = faster than the bus.
'Boleh saya lihat kamarnya?' asks permission – and 'boleh' alone is also the answer: 'Boleh!' = sure, go ahead. One word for both the asking and the granting.
'Bisa minta peta?' is the complete everyday request – no subject, no 'give me' verb. 'Minta' = ask for a thing; 'bisa' softens it into 'can I get...?'
'Tadi' = earlier today: 'tadi saya sudah beli' = I already bought (it) earlier.
'Jangan lupa' = don't forget, the go-to reminder opener: 'jangan lupa bawa paspor'. 'Jangan' negates commands; 'tidak lupa' would just describe someone who doesn't forget.
'Tolong' + verb = please (do something): 'tolong antar' = please take (it) there.
The 'me-' prefix turns a root into an active verb: 'inap' (stay over) becomes 'menginap' = to stay overnight. 'Kami menginap di hotel' = we stayed at a hotel.
'Kita' includes the person you're talking to, 'kami' leaves them out – 'kita istirahat' works because the listener is invited to rest too.
'Yang' also points back to things: 'laporan yang kamu kirim' = the report you sent.
English 'can' does double duty; Indonesian splits it: 'boleh' = allowed to, 'bisa' = able to. 'Boleh saya pulang?' asks permission, not ability.
'Paling lambat' (literally: slowest) sets a deadline: 'paling lambat hari Jumat' = by Friday at the latest.
The ending '-kan' turns a word into a doing-verb: 'jelas' (clear) → 'jelaskan' = explain.
'Akan' marks the future, but a time word can carry it alone: with 'besok' in the sentence, 'kami akan rapat' could drop the 'akan'. It just makes the future explicit.
The ending '-i' aims the action at someone: 'kabar' (news) → 'kabari' = let (someone) know.
